content: Preterm infants are born with insufficient glycogen reserves and require an increased glucose intake to match the rates of fetal growth and development. While breast milk offers numerous benefits for preterm infants, it may not fully meet the nutritional demands of these rapidly growing neonates. Supplementing human milk with carbohydrates has been proposed as a potential strategy to address this gap. However, there is a lack of robust data evaluating the benefits or potential harms of carbohydrate supplementation in human milk for promoting growth in preterm infants. This review represents a 2020 update of a Cochrane Review originally published in 1999. The objective of this review was to determine whether supplementing human milk with carbohydrates, compared to unsupplemented human milk, improves growth, body composition, and cardio-metabolic and neurodevelopmental outcomes in preterm infants, without causing significant adverse effects. The search strategy employed the standard methods of Cochrane Neonatal, including searches of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL 2019, Issue 8) and MEDLINE via PubMed as of August 22, 2019. Additional searches were conducted in clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials. Eligible studies included published and unpublished controlled trials that used random or quasi-random methods to allocate preterm infants in hospital settings to receive either human milk supplemented with carbohydrates or unsupplemented human milk. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the quality of the trials and evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Meta-analyses were planned using risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A fixed-effect model was intended for use, and sensitivity analyses were planned to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. Only one unblinded, quasi-randomized controlled trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial evaluated the effects of carbohydrate supplementation in the form of a prebiotic in 75 preterm infants. Two publications of the same trial were identified, but they reported conflicting methods regarding blinding and randomization. The study authors confirmed that both publications referred to the same trial but did not clarify which methodological description was accurate. The analysis of this trial provided very low-certainty evidence regarding the effect of carbohydrate supplementation on weight gain by 30 days of age (MD 160.4 grams, 95% CI 12.4 to 308.4 grams). There was no observed effect on the risk of feeding intolerance (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.15) or necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) (RR 0.2, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.3). The duration of hospital stay was shorter in the prebiotic group compared to the control group, with a median difference of 9 days. However, no data were available to assess the effects of carbohydrate supplementation on long-term growth or neurodevelopmental outcomes. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether carbohydrate supplementation of human milk has any meaningful impact on outcomes in preterm infants. The single included trial provided very low-quality evidence, and the study methods and analyses were reported with uncertainty. Additionally, the findings may have limited generalizability due to the small sample size and single-center design of the trial. Future research could explore the safety and efficacy of various types and concentrations of carbohydrate supplementation in preterm infants fed human milk. However, further trials specifically investigating digestible carbohydrates may not be conducted, as carbohydrate supplementation is already incorporated into multi-nutrient human milk fortifiers currently in use.
